value.overview: The Olive-sided Flycatcher (Contopus cooperi) is a large, strongly built North American flycatcher known for its distinctive “quick, three beers” song and habit of hunting from exposed treetops. It breeds mainly in boreal and montane coniferous forests, especially where forest openings, wetlands, streams, burns, or dead trees provide abundant flying insects. It undertakes a remarkably long migration to Central and South America. In Costa Rica, it is primarily encountered as a passage migrant rather than a regular breeding species.
value.classification: The Olive-sided Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers. Its scientific name is Contopus cooperi.
value.identification: This is a relatively large flycatcher with a broad, heavy-based bill, a dark olive-gray back, and a dark head. The sides of the breast and flanks are blackish or deep olive, contrasting with a conspicuous white patch down the center of the breast and white tufts on the lower back that may show beside the folded wings. The tail is broad and slightly notched. Its emphatic, three-part whistle is often the easiest way to detect it.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds from Alaska across much of Canada and in parts of the western and northeastern United States. It migrates through Mexico and Central America to wintering areas in northern South America. In Costa Rica, the Olive-sided Flycatcher is mainly a migrant, with records during spring and fall passage; it may use second-growth woodland, forest edges, open forest, and other semi-open habitats with prominent perches. It is not generally considered a resident or breeding species there.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Birds pass through Costa Rica during migration, and the country is part of the species’ Central American route between North American breeding grounds and South American wintering areas. It is generally uncommon and seasonal in Costa Rica rather than a regular year-round resident.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs primarily in open or edge habitats within boreal, montane, and western coniferous forests. Suitable sites often include dead or dying trees, stream margins, wetlands, bogs, recent burns, beaver ponds, or other natural openings that provide exposed hunting and singing perches. The nest is a small cup placed on a horizontal branch, usually well above the ground and often near the end of a branch. The species does not normally breed in Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: The Olive-sided Flycatcher feeds mainly on flying insects captured in aerial sallies from a high, exposed perch. Its prey includes bees, wasps, flying ants, beetles, dragonflies, grasshoppers, moths, and other flies. It often returns to the same perch after each attack and favors forest openings, edges, wetlands, and waterways where insect concentrations are high. Small amounts of fruit may occasionally be eaten during migration or on the wintering grounds.
value.behavior: This flycatcher is usually solitary and conspicuous when perched on the top of a dead tree or other prominent snag. It frequently scans from one favored lookout and launches upward or outward to catch insects before returning. The species is generally less associated with mixed-species feeding flocks than many smaller flycatchers. Its loud, distinctive song is commonly delivered from an exposed perch during the breeding season, while migrants may be quiet and difficult to detect.

conservation.populationTrend: The population has undergone a marked long-term decline across much of its range. Recent trends appear more stable in some areas, but the species remains vulnerable because of its relatively small population and dependence on suitable habitats across several countries and seasons.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include loss and degradation of mature forest and forest-edge habitat on the breeding and wintering grounds, especially in Central and South America. Fire suppression, removal of standing dead trees, salvage logging after fires, and changes to natural forest disturbance can reduce breeding habitat and foraging perches. Habitat loss along migration routes may also affect the species. Because Olive-sided Flycatchers pass through Costa Rica, protecting wooded stopover habitat there can support the wider migratory population.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect mature forests, forest edges, wetlands, and wooded riparian corridors used during migration and on the wintering grounds. Retain suitable standing dead trees where public safety allows, and avoid unnecessary removal of snags in natural forest areas. Support conservation of forests in Costa Rica and throughout the species’ breeding and wintering range. Bird monitoring and reporting of migration records can help clarify local timing, abundance, and habitat use.
